analysis.one_liner: Puts clear nutrition and warning labels on the front of packaged food and cracks down on misleading health claims.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote after being referred there in April 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require packaged foods to carry a standardized, easy-to-read summary of calories, added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat on the front of the package. It would force foods marketed as 'whole grain,' 'fruit,' 'vegetable,' or 'yogurt' to disclose how much of those ingredients they actually contain, define the term 'natural,' require caffeine and allergen disclosures, and make all label information available in a public FDA database and on online store pages. Foods sold on websites could not hide this information or charge extra for it.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers, including people with food allergies and celiac disease, who would see at a glance what is actually in a product instead of deciphering back-of-package fine print. Parents buying toddler drinks and people shopping for groceries online would also get clearer, mandatory information.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Grocery shoppers and people with allergies

how_it_helps.text: Requires a standardized symbol system on the front of every package showing calories, added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat, designed so consumers can compare products at a glance without nutrition expertise.

Products claiming to contain whole grains, fruit, vegetables, or yogurt must disclose the actual amount of those ingredients on the front of the package, stopping products with little real fruit from trading on the image.

Requires foods with artificial dyes, added sweeteners, caffeine, phosphorus, sugar alcohols, or gluten to state so prominently, gives FDA authority to add new major allergens to mandatory labeling, and requires allergen information on signs next to unpackaged food at retail.

Requires manufacturers to submit all label information to FDA in a public, searchable database, and requires online sellers to display nutrition, ingredient, and allergen information before purchase, with civil penalties up to $1 million for platforms that block or charge for it.
Requires FDA to define the term 'natural' and tighten standards for 'healthy' claims, including barring 'healthy' labels on grain products unless all grains are whole.

analysis.who_pays: Packaged food and beverage manufacturers, who face redesign and compliance costs and would lose some of their most effective marketing phrases; retailers and e-commerce platforms, which face new disclosure duties and fines.
analysis.who_pays_short: Packaged food makers and online grocers

drawbacks.text: Repackaging, reformulation, and database-submission requirements fall on all food manufacturers, and compliance costs are typically passed to consumers through higher prices; the bill gives exemptions only for small packages, not small businesses.

The bill itself anticipates a side effect: labeling pressure can push manufacturers toward low- and no-calorie sweeteners, and it requires a report on whether that substitution rises to a level with negative health consequences.

The regulatory burden is heavy and the timelines aggressive—proposed rules within a year and final rules within two, with automatic take-effect if FDA misses deadlines—raising the risk of rushed, poorly calibrated rules.

New front-of-package warnings for dyes, sweeteners, and sugar alcohols could clutter labels and, by stigmatizing legal ingredients, invite years of litigation over the 'artificial' definitions the bill writes into statute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real and broad: honest front-of-package information addresses a genuine information gap that shapes diet-related disease, and the allergen and online-disclosure provisions help people who currently have no practical way to check a label. The costs are compliance costs for a large industry and some risk of over-broad warnings, which is why the bill leans on FDA rulemaking to set details. The design is generally sound, but its aggressive deadlines and industry-wide mandates would have made for a contested rulemaking fight.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it, read it twice, sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and no action ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on April 26, 2023 with four Democratic cosponsors: Senators Whitehouse, Markey, Booker, and Cardin.
On the day of introduction the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That was the bill's last recorded action; the committee never held a hearing or markup, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged food and beverage makers are better off: they keep the current labels and marketing terms the bill would have restricted, and avoid the compliance costs and the public database of label information. Shoppers are left with the status quo labeling system the bill called inadequate.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Food Labeling Modernization Act of 2023 in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse, Edward Markey, Cory Booker, and Benjamin Cardin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republicans joined.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 26, 2023 and took no further action—no hearing, markup, or vote—for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Food and beverage industry trade groups
against.role: Manufacturers of packaged foods subject to the labeling rules
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed front-of-package labeling mandates and restrictions on terms like 'natural' in federal and state food-labeling fights, and had no incentive to press Congress to move the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Senate Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; there was never a vote, so no roll-call record exists, but the bill's Democratic-only sponsorship shaped its prospects in a Senate that required 60 votes to advance most legislation.

industries.note: The bill mandates front-of-package nutrition symbols, restricts health claims and terms like 'natural,' and forces submission of all label information to a public FDA database. Label redesign, reformulation, and compliance costs fall on manufacturers, and marketing claims that let lightly fruited or refined-grain products look healthy would be curbed.

industries.industry: Online grocery retailers and e-commerce platforms
industries.note: Platforms must show nutrition, ingredient, and allergen information prominently before purchase, cannot charge extra for it, and face civil penalties up to $1 million per proceeding for violations. This is a direct disclosure mandate on a channel where consumers currently often cannot see a label at all.

Brick-and-mortar retailers would face new duties to post allergen signs for unpackaged foods but benefit little or lose little on packaged goods, where manufacturers bear the label changes. Retailers largely pass labeling costs through.
